title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 17
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A garage offers a free inspection with every service and reports that customers who accept the inspection spend more on repairs than those who decline it. The owner concludes that the inspection persuades customers to maintain their vehicles properly.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Customers who accept the inspection are those who suspect something is wrong with their vehicle.
B. The inspection takes twenty minutes.
C. Some repairs are carried out by other garages.
D. The garage advertises the inspection in its window.
E. Inspections are carried out by qualified mechanics.
questions.explanation: The acceptance decision selects vehicles already thought to have faults, so higher repair spending need reflect no persuasion at all.

questions.prompt: A hotel introduced a strict cancellation policy and reports that its occupancy rate has risen. Management concludes that guests who book are now more likely to arrive.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How much the hotel charges for a room
B. Whether guests were informed of the policy at booking
C. Whether the number of bookings made has changed since the policy was introduced
D. How many rooms the hotel has
E. Whether competitors have similar policies
questions.explanation: Occupancy is arrivals over rooms; if bookings fell while no-shows fell more, the reading is different from a policy that simply deterred bookings and coincided with other demand. Without the booking figure the conclusion cannot be assessed.

questions.prompt: A distribution centre introduced a night shift and reports that orders are now dispatched faster on average. A consultant argues that the improvement may not persist.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most supports the consultant's argument?
options: A. Night shift workers are paid a premium.
B. Some staff have transferred from the day shift.
C. Dispatch times are measured automatically.
D. The centre serves customers in several time zones.
E. The night shift is currently clearing a backlog accumulated before it began, and once that is exhausted its capacity will exceed the orders arriving overnight.
questions.explanation: A one-off stock of work explains the current improvement and predicts its end, which is exactly the persistence question.

questions.prompt: A city installed parcel lockers and reports that failed home deliveries in the surrounding streets have fallen by a third. The council concludes that lockers reduce failed deliveries.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. Lockers are cheaper to install than delivery offices.
B. In comparable streets elsewhere in the city where no lockers were installed, failed deliveries were unchanged over the same period.
C. Some residents use lockers for returns as well.
D. Couriers report that lockers are convenient.
E. The lockers are open at all hours.
questions.explanation: A matched comparison rules out city-wide changes in courier practice or shopping volume as the explanation.

questions.prompt: Every consultant at the Marchmont clinic who runs a weekend list has a waiting time under twelve weeks. No consultant with a waiting time under twelve weeks has patients transferred to another hospital. Some consultants at the clinic have patients transferred to another hospital.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Weekend lists reduce waiting times.
B. Most consultants run weekend lists.
C. No patient at the clinic waits more than twelve weeks.
D. Some consultants at the clinic do not run a weekend list.
E. Consultants with transfers have the longest lists.
questions.explanation: Consultants with transfers have waits of twelve weeks or more, and a weekend list implies a shorter wait, so those consultants run no weekend list. B is a causal claim the statements do not license.

questions.prompt: A restaurant began requiring a deposit for reservations and reports that its no-show rate fell from 15 per cent to 3 per cent. The owner concludes that most no-shows had been deliberate.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the administrative cost of taking deposits
B. does not report the number of reservations
C. assumes a deposit distinguishes deliberate no-shows from those caused by illness, traffic or forgetfulness
D. overlooks customers who book at several restaurants
E. relies on a single restaurant's experience
questions.explanation: A deposit raises the cost of every kind of failure to attend, including the accidental ones, so the fall does not establish what the original no-shows consisted of.

questions.prompt: A garden centre found that plants displayed near the entrance sell faster than those at the rear, and plans to move its slowest-selling plants to the entrance in order to sell them.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. The entrance display is refreshed weekly.
B. The rear of the centre is under cover.
C. Some customers browse the whole centre before buying.
D. The centre has always placed its most popular seasonal plants at the entrance, and customers come in intending to buy them.
E. Plants at the entrance are visible from the car park.
questions.explanation: If position has been assigned by expected popularity, the sales difference reflects the plants rather than the location, and moving unpopular stock there need not sell it.

questions.prompt: A driving school reports that its pupils pass the practical test at a higher rate than the national average and advertises its instruction as more effective.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advertisement?
options: A. The school requires pupils to pass an internal assessment before it will book their test, and pupils who fail it are not entered.
B. The school charges more per lesson than most competitors.
C. Some pupils take lessons elsewhere as well.
D. The national average includes candidates with no professional instruction.
E. The school operates in several towns.
questions.explanation: Screening who is entered raises the pass rate without any change in teaching, and the advertised comparison is with a population that was not screened.

questions.prompt: A sports club raised its annual subscription and reports that total subscription income rose, concluding that its members are insensitive to price.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The club has a waiting list.
B. The increase was announced six months in advance.
C. Some members pay monthly.
D. Comparable clubs charge more.
E. A fifth of members did not renew, and the club's coaching sessions are now under-attended, but the higher fee from remaining members more than offset the loss.
questions.explanation: A substantial loss of members is exactly price sensitivity; revenue rose because the remaining demand was inelastic enough to compensate, which is a different claim.

questions.prompt: A water company reports that it repaired 40 per cent more leaks last year than the year before, and presents this as evidence of improved performance.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the presentation?
options: A. The company employs more repair crews than before.
B. Total water lost from the network rose over the same period, as the number of new leaks grew faster than repairs.
C. Some leaks are reported by members of the public.
D. Repair costs rose in line with the number of repairs.
E. The network is older than most in the country.
questions.explanation: Repairs completed is an activity measure; the outcome the company exists to manage moved in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: A bakery removed the seating from its shop to make room for more display counters, and its takings rose. The owner concludes that customers prefer to buy and leave.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the cost of removing the seating
B. does not consider customers who never visited the shop
C. treats a rise in takings as evidence about preference, when more display space alone could raise sales
D. assumes takings are recorded accurately
E. overlooks seasonal variation in demand
questions.explanation: Two changes happened at once — less seating, more display — and the second is sufficient to explain the takings without any claim about what customers prefer.

questions.passageText:
Tying executive pay to share price is intended to align the interests of managers with those of owners. The instrument is cruder than the intention, and the reason is that a share price moves for reasons having nothing to do with the executive.

When an oil company's shares rise because the oil price rose, an executive paid in shares is rewarded for a movement that would have occurred under any management. The standard remedy is relative performance evaluation: reward the executive for outperforming a benchmark of comparable firms, which removes the industry-wide component. The remedy is well understood, straightforward to implement, and used far less than the theory predicts — a gap the literature has documented for decades and explained less convincingly than it has measured.

Two further problems attach to any measure. Executives influence what is measured through choices whose effects arrive later than their tenure: deferring maintenance, cutting research, repurchasing shares. And a target set on a single number invites management of that number rather than of the business, which is the general failure of any indicator used as a target.

Longer vesting periods address part of this by extending the horizon over which a decision's consequences are captured. They do not address selection of the benchmark, and they cannot address the deepest difficulty, which is that the contribution of a single executive to a large firm's performance is not separately observable. Pay arrangements are therefore not measurements. They are bets on a proxy, and the useful questions concern how good the proxy is and who bears the cost when it is wrong.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, relative performance evaluation is intended to
options: A. remove the component of share price movement common to comparable firms
B. increase the total value of executive pay
C. shorten the period over which pay is assessed
D. replace share-based pay with cash
E. reduce the influence of shareholders on pay decisions
questions.explanation: That is precisely the remedy described for rewarding executives for movements they did not cause.

questions.passageText:
That patients given an inert treatment often improve is not in dispute. What that improvement consists of is disputed, and the popular formulation — that belief heals — states considerably more than the evidence supports.

Several distinct things are bundled together in a measured placebo response. Many conditions improve without treatment, so a patient who joins a trial when symptoms are at their worst will tend to be better later regardless of what they receive. Reporting effects contribute: patients tell an attentive researcher what they think is expected, and outcomes that depend on self-report move more than outcomes that do not. Separating these from any genuine effect of expectation requires a comparison the standard trial does not include, namely a group given no treatment at all.

Where such three-armed studies have been run, the picture is uneven. Placebo effects on pain, nausea and anxiety are real and measurable, with plausible mechanisms including expectation-driven release of endogenous opioids. Effects on objective measures — tumour size, cholesterol, lung function — are small or absent. The distinction is not arbitrary: it tracks the difference between what a nervous system can modulate and what it cannot.

This has a clinical consequence often stated backwards. That a treatment works no better than placebo does not mean it works through belief and is therefore useful anyway; it means the trial cannot distinguish it from the natural course of the illness plus the effect of being treated attentively. Those are different claims, and only one of them is a reason to prescribe.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, distinguishing a genuine effect of expectation from other contributions requires
options: A. a larger sample
B. a group given no treatment at all
C. a longer follow-up period
D. measuring only self-reported outcomes
E. excluding patients whose symptoms are severe
questions.explanation: Without a no-treatment arm, natural improvement and reporting effects cannot be separated from expectation.

questions.passageText:
Two independent methods exist for measuring crime, and they disagree in ways that are informative rather than embarrassing.

Police records count offences reported to and recorded by the police. Their weakness is that both steps are variable: many offences are never reported, and recording practice differs by force and changes over time. A rise in recorded crime is therefore consistent with more crime, with more reporting, or with a change in recording rules — and campaigns encouraging victims to come forward reliably raise the recorded figure for the offences they concern, which is the intended outcome and looks like deterioration.

Victimisation surveys ask a large sample whether they have experienced particular offences. They capture unreported crime and are unaffected by recording practice, which makes them the better instrument for trends in common offences. Their limitations are structural: they miss crimes against businesses and against those not in households, they rely on respondents recalling and classifying events correctly, and their samples are too small to say much about rare offences, including homicide, for which police and health records are far better.

The disciplined approach uses each where it is strong and treats divergence as a question rather than a contradiction. When survey-measured crime falls while recorded crime rises, the most probable reading is a change in reporting or recording rather than two contradictory facts — and a commentator citing whichever series supports their case, without addressing the other, is not making an argument about crime.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a rise in recorded crime is consistent with all of the following EXCEPT
options: A. a fall in the number of offences experienced by households
B. an increase in offences committed
C. an increase in reporting by victims
D. a change in police recording rules
E. a successful campaign encouraging victims to come forward
questions.explanation: The first four are the readings the passage explicitly permits. A fall in offences experienced is what the survey measures and is not among the explanations of a rise in the recorded series.

questions.passageText:
Almost no classical text survives in a copy made by its author. What survives is a chain of manuscripts, each copied from another, and the discipline that reconstructs the relationships between them tells us more about the transmission than most readers assume.

The method depends on error. A scribe copying by hand introduces mistakes, and a manuscript copied from that one inherits them along with new ones. Shared errors therefore indicate shared ancestry, and a family tree of surviving manuscripts can be built from the pattern of agreement in error rather than from agreement in correct readings, which proves nothing about descent. From that tree an editor reconstructs, where possible, the readings of the lost ancestor.

The method's limits are well known to its practitioners. Scribes corrected as well as corrupted, and a scribe comparing two exemplars produces a manuscript with mixed ancestry that the tree cannot represent. Some errors are so natural that different scribes make them independently. And the reconstruction reaches the earliest recoverable ancestor of the surviving copies, which may be centuries later than the author and may already contain corruption invisible to the method.

What this yields is a text with a documented history rather than an authentic original. A good edition prints the reconstruction and records the alternatives, so a reader can see where the evidence was thin and what was chosen. That apparatus, which non-specialists usually skip, is the part that distinguishes a scholarly edition from a confident one.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the relationships between manuscripts are reconstructed from
options: A. agreement in correct readings
B. the physical age of the parchment
C. shared errors, which indicate shared ancestry
D. the reputation of the copying centre
E. the completeness of each copy
questions.explanation: The passage says agreement in correct readings proves nothing about descent.

From that tree an editor reconstructs, where possible, the readings of the lost ancestor.

The method's limits are well known to its practitioners. Scribes corrected as well as corrupted, and a scribe comparing two exemplars produces a manuscript with mixed ancestry that the tree cannot represent. Some errors are so natural that different scribes make them independently. And the reconstruction reaches the earliest recoverable ancestor of the surviving copies, which may be centuries later than the author and may already contain corruption invisible to the method.

What this yields is a text with a documented history rather than an authentic original. A good edition prints the reconstruction and records the alternatives, so a reader can see where the evidence was thin and what was chosen. That apparatus, which non-specialists usually skip, is the part that distinguishes a scholarly edition from a confident one.
